name: Isle of Skye
shortDescription: The largest of the Inner Hebrides, famed for the Cuillin mountains, dramatic coastlines, and the Old Man of Storr.
history: Skye has been inhabited since the Mesolithic. Norse rule lasted until 1266, after which the island fell under the MacLeod and MacDonald clans. The Highland Clearances of the 19th century reshaped its population.
geography: Skye is the second-largest Scottish island. The Cuillin range dominates the south, while the Trotternish peninsula in the north is famed for landslip features such as the Quiraing and the Storr.
transport: Connected to the mainland by the Skye Bridge from Kyle of Lochalsh. Ferries run from Mallaig to Armadale and from Glenelg to Kylerhea. Local buses link Portree, Broadford, Uig and Dunvegan.
accommodation: Wide range from hotels in Portree to B&Bs, hostels and self-catering cottages across the island. Booking ahead is essential in summer.

name: Lewis and Harris
shortDescription: The largest island in Scotland, with the rolling moorland of Lewis in the north and the rugged hills of Harris in the south.
history: Home to the Neolithic Callanish Standing Stones and Iron Age brochs. Norse settlement left a lasting linguistic legacy in place names. Stornoway has been the regional capital since the 16th century.
geography: A single landmass split by tradition into Lewis (low-lying, peat-covered) and Harris (mountainous, with white-sand beaches such as Luskentyre).
transport: CalMac ferries from Ullapool to Stornoway, and from Uig (Skye) to Tarbert. Loganair flies into Stornoway from Glasgow, Edinburgh and Inverness.
accommodation: Hotels and guest houses in Stornoway and Tarbert, plus crofts and self-catering across both islands.

name: Mainland (Orkney)
shortDescription: The largest of the Orkney Islands, dense with Neolithic monuments including Skara Brae, Maeshowe and the Ring of Brodgar.
history: Continuously inhabited for over 8,500 years. Skara Brae predates Stonehenge and the Pyramids. Norse rule until 1468, when Orkney was pledged to Scotland as part of a royal dowry.
geography: Low-lying and fertile, with sea cliffs at Yesnaby and Marwick Head. Surrounded by the smaller North and South Isles.
transport: NorthLink ferries from Aberdeen and Scrabster to Stromness or Kirkwall; Pentland Ferries from Gills Bay to St Margaret's Hope. Loganair flies into Kirkwall.
accommodation: Hotels in Kirkwall and Stromness, plus B&Bs and self-catering across the island.

name: Mainland (Shetland)
shortDescription: Britain's most northerly large island, closer to Bergen than to Edinburgh, with deep voes, sea cliffs and Up Helly Aa fire festivals.
history: Norse from the 9th century until pledged to Scotland in 1469. Jarlshof shows continuous habitation from the Bronze Age to the Viking era.
geography: A long, narrow island shaped by glaciation and the sea, with the dramatic cliffs of Eshaness and the sand tombolo of St Ninian's Isle.
transport: NorthLink overnight ferry from Aberdeen to Lerwick. Loganair flies into Sumburgh from Aberdeen, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Inverness and Kirkwall.
accommodation: Hotels in Lerwick, plus camping böds, guest houses and self-catering across the island.

name: Isle of Mull
shortDescription: Mountainous Inner Hebridean island known for white-tailed eagles, the colourful waterfront of Tobermory, and the gateway to Iona and Staffa.
history: Long associated with Clan MacLean and Duart Castle. Iona, off Mull's western tip, was the cradle of Christianity in Scotland under St Columba.
geography: Largely volcanic in origin, dominated by Ben More, the only Munro in the Hebrides outside Skye. Indented coastline with sea lochs.
transport: CalMac ferries from Oban to Craignure, Lochaline to Fishnish, and Kilchoan to Tobermory.
accommodation: Hotels and guest houses in Tobermory and Craignure, plus cottages and bothies across the island.

name: Islay
shortDescription: The 'Queen of the Hebrides', world-famous for its peated single malt whiskies and rich birdlife.
history: Seat of the Lordship of the Isles in the medieval period, ruled from Finlaggan. Whisky distilling has shaped its modern economy.
geography: Lower-lying than its neighbours, with extensive peat moor, sea lochs and beaches. Home to over 100 species of breeding birds.
transport: CalMac ferries from Kennacraig to Port Ellen and Port Askaig. Loganair flies into Islay Airport from Glasgow.
accommodation: Hotels in Bowmore, Port Ellen and Port Charlotte, plus distillery-owned guest houses and cottages.

name: Isle of Arran
shortDescription: Often called 'Scotland in miniature', combining Highland-style mountains in the north with rolling Lowland scenery in the south.
history: Brodick Castle was the ancient seat of the Hamilton family. The island has Bronze Age stone circles at Machrie Moor.
geography: Bisected geologically by the Highland Boundary Fault. Goat Fell dominates the skyline above Brodick Bay.
transport: CalMac ferry from Ardrossan to Brodick (around 55 minutes), plus a summer service from Claonaig to Lochranza.
accommodation: Hotels in Brodick and Lamlash, plus B&Bs, hostels and self-catering across the island.

name: Isle of Bute
shortDescription: A gentle, accessible Clyde island with the Victorian resort town of Rothesay and the Gothic-revival Mount Stuart House.
history: Long associated with the Stuart royal family. Rothesay grew as a steamer-era resort for Glaswegians 'doon the watter'.
geography: Crossed by the Highland Boundary Fault, giving it both Highland and Lowland character within a small area.
transport: CalMac ferries from Wemyss Bay to Rothesay and from Colintraive to Rhubodach.
accommodation: Hotels and guest houses in Rothesay, plus self-catering across the island.

name: Iona
shortDescription: Tiny island off Mull's western tip; the spiritual cradle of Christianity in Scotland and home to Iona Abbey.
history: St Columba founded a monastery here in 563 AD. The Book of Kells is thought to have originated on Iona.
geography: Just 1.5 miles wide, with white shell-sand beaches and the marble quarry at the southern tip.
transport: Passenger ferry from Fionnphort on Mull (10-minute crossing). No private cars allowed for visitors.
accommodation: Limited to a couple of hotels and a handful of B&Bs and self-catering cottages — book well ahead.

name: Staffa
shortDescription: Uninhabited basalt island famed for Fingal's Cave, whose hexagonal columns inspired Mendelssohn's overture.
history: Sir Joseph Banks 'rediscovered' Staffa for science in 1772; Queen Victoria, Walter Scott, Wordsworth and Verne all visited.
geography: Formed by the same Palaeocene lava flow as Northern Ireland's Giant's Causeway. Fingal's Cave is 20 m high and 70 m deep.
transport: Day boat trips from Mull (Fionnphort or Ulva Ferry) and from Iona, weather permitting.
accommodation: None — visited as a day trip only.

name: Isle of Man
shortDescription: Self-governing Crown Dependency in the middle of the Irish Sea, famed for the TT motorcycle races and the Manx Gaelic language.
history: Home to Tynwald, often described as the world's oldest continuous parliament (founded c. 979 AD). Norse rule until 1266.
geography: A central upland of slate and shale, with sea cliffs at the Calf of Man and the Sound. The island has its own Manx cat and four-horned Loaghtan sheep.
transport: Steam Packet ferries from Heysham, Liverpool, Belfast and Dublin. Flights into Ronaldsway from many UK and Irish airports.
accommodation: Full range of hotels, guest houses, hostels and self-catering, with a long Victorian seaside tradition in Douglas.

name: Anglesey (Ynys Môn)
shortDescription: The largest Welsh island, separated from the mainland by the Menai Strait and crossed by Telford's and Stephenson's bridges.
history: An ancient druidic stronghold attacked by the Romans in 60 AD. Beaumaris Castle is one of Edward I's 'iron ring' fortresses.
geography: Mostly low-lying farmland, fringed by an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty coastline. Holy Island, joined by causeway, hosts the port of Holyhead.
transport: Crossed by the A55 expressway via the Britannia Bridge. Holyhead is a major ferry port for Dublin and Dún Laoghaire. Trains run to Holyhead from London Euston.
accommodation: Hotels, holiday parks, cottages and B&Bs across the island — popular for family holidays.

name: Isle of Wight
shortDescription: Diamond-shaped island off Hampshire, famous for the Needles, Osborne House and one of Europe's largest music festivals.
history: Queen Victoria's beloved Osborne House made the island a fashionable resort. Cowes has hosted yacht racing since 1826.
geography: A chalk ridge runs east–west, ending in the iconic Needles sea stacks. Half the island is designated AONB.
transport: Wightlink and Red Funnel ferries from Portsmouth, Southampton and Lymington; Hovertravel hovercraft from Southsea to Ryde.
accommodation: Hundreds of hotels, holiday parks, B&Bs and self-catering options across the island.

name: St Mary's (Isles of Scilly)
shortDescription: The largest of the subtropical-feeling Isles of Scilly, 28 miles south-west of Land's End.
history: Inhabited since the Bronze Age, with hundreds of chambered cairns. The Civil War saw Royalist holdouts here until 1651.
geography: Granite island fringed by white-sand beaches. The Scillies as a whole enjoy one of the mildest climates in the British Isles.
transport: Scillonian III ferry from Penzance, plus Skybus flights from Land's End, Newquay and Exeter to St Mary's Airport.
accommodation: Hotels in Hugh Town, plus campsites, B&Bs and cottages. The other inhabited islands have their own accommodation.

name: Lundy
shortDescription: Granite island in the Bristol Channel; a marine nature reserve owned by the National Trust and run by the Landmark Trust.
history: Once a pirate stronghold under the Marisco family in the 13th century. The Heaven family ran it as a private kingdom in the 19th century.
geography: A 3-mile long granite plateau rising to 122 m of cliffs on the western side. Famed for puffins (which give the island its Norse name).
transport: MS Oldenburg sails from Bideford or Ilfracombe (March–October). Helicopter service from Hartland Point in winter.
accommodation: 23 Landmark Trust holiday properties, a campsite, and the Marisco Tavern. No day visitors stay overnight in private accommodation.

name: Rathlin Island
shortDescription: Northern Ireland's only permanently inhabited offshore island, famed for its seabird colonies and the Robert the Bruce cave.
history: Site of an early Christian monastery and the 1575 Rathlin Island massacre. Robert the Bruce reputedly took refuge in a cave here in 1306.
geography: L-shaped island of chalk and basalt, with three lighthouses and the RSPB West Light Seabird Centre.
transport: Rathlin Ferries operates a passenger and small-vehicle service from Ballycastle (around 25 minutes by fast ferry).
accommodation: A handful of guest houses, self-catering cottages and a campsite. Limited capacity — book early.

name: Jersey
shortDescription: Largest of the Channel Islands, 14 miles from the French coast — a Crown Dependency with its own parliament and currency.
history: Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933, retained by the English Crown after 1204. Occupied by Germany 1940–1945.
geography: A south-tilting plateau with extensive sandy bays in the south and rocky cliffs in the north. Famously huge tidal range.
transport: Condor Ferries from Poole and Portsmouth; multiple daily flights into Jersey Airport from across the UK and Europe.
accommodation: Wide range of hotels, guest houses and self-catering across the island; St Helier is the main hub.

name: Guernsey
shortDescription: Second-largest Channel Island, with the picturesque harbour of St Peter Port and a strong maritime tradition.
history: Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. Occupied 1940–1945 — Castle Cornet's German fortifications still stand.
geography: Higher and more cliff-bound in the south, lower and beachier in the north. The Bailiwick also includes Sark, Herm and Alderney.
transport: Condor Ferries from Poole and Portsmouth; flights into Guernsey Airport from across the UK and Europe.
accommodation: Hotels, guest houses and self-catering across the island, concentrated around St Peter Port.

name: Brownsea Island
shortDescription: National Trust island in Poole Harbour, birthplace of the Scout movement and a stronghold for native red squirrels.
history: Robert Baden-Powell held the first experimental Scout camp here in August 1907. Owned by the National Trust since 1962.
geography: Wooded island with heath, lagoon and saltmarsh. One of the few places in southern England with red squirrels.
transport: Frequent passenger boats from Poole Quay and Sandbanks (March–October). No vehicles on the island.
accommodation: John Lewis-run holiday flats and a campsite — booked direct via the operators.

name: Lindisfarne (Holy Island)
shortDescription: Tidal island off the Northumberland coast, cradle of Celtic Christianity in England and home to the iconic Lindisfarne Castle.
history: St Aidan founded a monastery here in 635 AD. The Lindisfarne Gospels were created here c. 700. Viking raids began in 793.
geography: Linked to the mainland by a causeway covered at high tide. Twice-daily 'safe crossing times' are published.
transport: Drive across the causeway from Beal — check tide tables. No public buses except seasonal services.
accommodation: A handful of small hotels, B&Bs and self-catering cottages in the village; book ahead.

name: Fair Isle
shortDescription: Britain's most remote inhabited island, midway between Orkney and Shetland — famed for knitwear, seabirds, and rare bird sightings.
history: Gifted to the National Trust for Scotland in 1954. The Fair Isle Bird Observatory has logged migrants since 1948.
geography: A small island of cliffs and crofts, often the first British landfall for vagrant birds blown off course from Scandinavia or America.
transport: Good Shepherd IV ferry from Grutness (Shetland Mainland), and Loganair flights from Tingwall (Lerwick) and Sumburgh.
accommodation: Limited self-catering and B&B; the new Bird Observatory is being rebuilt after a 2019 fire.

name: St Kilda (Hirta)
shortDescription: Remote, dual UNESCO World Heritage Site 41 miles west of the Outer Hebrides; evacuated in 1930 and now home only to a small military and conservation team.
history: Continuous habitation from prehistory until the surviving 36 islanders requested evacuation on 29 August 1930. Bequeathed to the National Trust for Scotland in 1957.
geography: Volcanic archipelago with the highest sea cliffs in the UK at Conachair (430 m). Home to nearly a million seabirds.
transport: No scheduled service. Day boats from Harris and Skye in summer (sea conditions permitting); cruise ships and private yachts visit.
accommodation: None for general visitors. National Trust working parties and researchers stay in restricted accommodation.

name: Inchcailloch
shortDescription: Wooded island in Loch Lomond, part of the Loch Lomond National Nature Reserve, with a circular trail and the ruined chapel of St Kentigerna.
history: Site of an 8th-century nunnery dedicated to St Kentigerna. The MacGregor clan burial ground remains in use.
geography: Mostly oak woodland; one of the inspirations for Loch Lomond National Park's conservation focus.
transport: Passenger ferry from Balmaha; canoe and kayak hire also available locally.
accommodation: Wild camping permitted at the designated Port Bawn site (permit required March–September).

name: Belle Isle (Windermere)
shortDescription: The largest of Windermere's islands and the only one ever permanently inhabited; site of England's first round house, built in 1774.
history: Privately owned by the Curwen family for over 200 years. The round house is Grade II* listed.
geography: A wooded, oval island roughly 1 km long in the centre of England's largest natural lake.
transport: Privately owned — viewable only from passing Windermere Lake Cruises ferries.
accommodation: Not open to the public; no accommodation available.

name: Eel Pie Island
shortDescription: Small inhabited island in the Thames at Twickenham, legendary for its 1960s music venue that hosted The Rolling Stones, The Who and Pink Floyd.
history: Named for the eel pies sold to day-trippers in the 19th century. The Eel Pie Island Hotel hosted seminal blues and R&B gigs from 1956 to 1967.
geography: Roughly 600 m long, with around 50 homes, two boatyards and a community of artists' studios.
transport: Footbridge from Twickenham Embankment — pedestrians only.
accommodation: Private residential — no public accommodation. Studios open twice yearly to visitors.

name: Isle of Dogs
shortDescription: Peninsula formed by a Thames meander in east London, technically an island since the West India Docks were cut across its neck in 1802; now home to Canary Wharf.
history: Marshland used for grazing in medieval times; transformed by the West India Docks (1802) and again by 1980s redevelopment into Europe's tallest financial district.
geography: A teardrop of land enclosed by the Thames; the docks effectively turn it into an island. Dominated by the towers of Canary Wharf.
transport: DLR, Jubilee line, Elizabeth line, Thames Clipper river bus, and the Greenwich foot tunnel under the river.
accommodation: Numerous hotels in and around Canary Wharf, plus serviced apartments — a major business-travel destination.

name: Burgh Island
shortDescription: Tidal island off the South Devon coast, famous for its 1929 art-deco hotel, the haunt of Agatha Christie, Noël Coward and the Beatles.
history: The Pilchard Inn dates to 1336. Agatha Christie wrote 'And Then There Were None' and 'Evil Under the Sun' here.
geography: Linked to Bigbury-on-Sea by a sand causeway at low tide and an unusual sea tractor at high tide.
transport: Walk across the causeway when the tide is out, or ride the sea tractor when it's in.
accommodation: The Burgh Island Hotel (rooms include 'The Beach House' suite); also the Pilchard Inn for food and drink.
